searches.note: Twenty eight searches of a share of twenty eight, none of them the author's. Nine were restricted to a house's own domain and are read as primary through their summaries: gruppoitalianovini.it twice (Santa Teresa's grapes and vineyard; the cellar's 1958 and its sixty years abroad), casteldepaolis.com twice (the story; the cellar and the cisterns), famigliacotarella.it twice (the history; the Montiano and Sodale sheets), casaledellaioria.com twice (the estate; Torre del Piano's sheet) and casaledelgiglio.it once (Mater Matuta's page, the Satricum page). Twelve blocked the author's own sources so that an independent account would show. The Frascati rules search is counted with Fontana Candida and serves Castel de Paolis too. No WebFetch was tried. Every record was tested; no fact that rests on no source was kept in a record marked checked.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the classification and its year, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

The searches went first to the houses' own pages and sheets for their own dates and methods and to the appellation texts, then to the press and the merchants, with the author's sources blocked where they would only have repeated themselves.

Where the sources corrected the record (Santa Teresa's making, Vigna Adriana's early Frascati label, the research partner's institution, one brother and not two, the rank of the first Montiano, the DOC of 1973, Cesanese di Affile's own DOC, the dig of 1896, the research of 1985) it was set right with its source; where a detail rested on one merchant or on nothing the refuter read (the fermentation temperature and hand picking of Santa Teresa, the old vines pulled up at Castel de Paolis, the Merlot clone of 1990, the next generation) it was cut.
A writer's own blog, met in several results, was read for orientation only and is cited nowhere; prices, scores, rankings, hectares and bottle counts were read and not used.

tested: The founding: the house's page (Gruppo Italiano Vini, read through search) dates its cellars to 1958 and says it has spread Frascati abroad for more than sixty years; Vinicum and DoctorWine give 1958 too. Confirmed, hedged as the house's account.
The hill and the cellar: Vinicum places the farmstead on the Fontana Candida hill at Monte Porzio Catone; the Roman villa said to be Horace's stays out (one account, told as perhaps).

Santa Teresa: the house's own wine page gives Malvasia del Lazio (Puntinata), Malvasia di Candia and Greco from its 13 hectare vineyard in the Santa Teresa district, on deep, sandy volcanic ash at 200 to 400 metres; the vineyard's size is volatile and stays out. Trebbiano in older vintages: Italian Wine Shop's 2015 notes (Trebbiano and Greco made off the skins, the Malvasia macerated cold for twelve hours) and the author's i-Italy for 2004. Confirmed.

The making: no technical sheet of the house gives a fermentation temperature; Etilika's 2024 listing gives steel at a controlled temperature, no skin maceration and no malolactic, Italian Wine Shop's 2015 notes keep the wine in temperature controlled steel until bottling. The 15 to 16 degrees Celsius and the hand picking rested on one merchant's sheet and were cut.

The rules: Italian Wine Central, Drink Italian and Accademia del Vino give the DOC of 1966 (D.P.R. of 16 May 1966), the DOCGs of Frascati Superiore and Cannellino by the decree of 20 September 2011 and at least seven tenths Malvasia di Candia and Malvasia del Lazio in every tier. Confirmed: the label term, the card and the traps stand.
Luna Mater: the house lists it as a Frascati Superiore DOCG Riserva among its grandi selezioni. Confirmed.
The serving temperature: listings give 8 to 10 and 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; 8 to 10 is kept, within the Codex's range for a light white.

The house rules: nobody living named (the group's manager of 2026, met on its page, is not named); no price, no score; the house page's claim to be the largest Frascati maker is not used; British; no dash. The questions: one key each, distractors of one kind (four methods; four years, 1932 the year of Littoria and 2011 the DOCG), the explanations teach.

tested: The house's story (read through search): the first parcel bought in 1974, the plots beside it in 1977, the grapes sold to the local co-operatives until 1985, many varieties native and international trialled from 1985 to 1993, the whole estate replanted between 1988 and 1993, and three whites released in 1993: Frascati DOC Campovecchio, Frascati Superiore and Donna Adriana. Confirmed; founded stays empty, since the house dates its land to 1974 and its wines to 1993 and others give 1985.

The research: Castelli Notizie and Gli Scomunicati say the founder was then an under secretary in the government, at the ministry of agriculture, and began the project in 1985 with a professor of viticulture; one account puts the professor at the Istituto Agrario di San Michele all'Adige in 1985, others at the University of Milan, so the record names no institution. The research is given as 1985 to 1992 by several accounts and 1985 to 1993 by the house; the record keeps the house's replanting years.

The old vines of Malvasia di Candia and Trebbiano pulled up: no source read names the varieties; Castelli Notizie speaks of a total uprooting, so the record says the whole estate was replanted and names no old vines.

Donna Adriana: the house's page gives Viognier with Malvasia Puntinata and a small share fermented in wood; a listing of the 2022 vintage gives Viognier about 80 per cent, Malvasia del Lazio the rest, 85 per cent in steel and 15 in barriques. The making keeps the house's 18 degrees Celsius and about a seventh in barriques; the taste of new oak denied was a judgement no source gave and was cut.

Vigna Adriana: Lavinium's producer profile lists Frascati Superiore Vigna Adriana for 1997 and 1998 and CellarTracker a 1998 Frascati Vigna Adriana; World of Fine Wine lists a Vigna Adriana Lazio Bianco IGT; WineNews gives the 2000 vintage as Malvasia Puntinata about four fifths with Viognier, a 2001 listing gives Viognier about four fifths. So the early vintages carried the Frascati name and the Viognier lead belongs to the later IGT wine; the record says so in the grapes, the label, the story and a new trap, and leaves the early blend out because the two listings disagree.

The cisterns: the house's cellar page tells of Roman water cisterns found beneath part of the cellar floor during works. Confirmed. The altitude of 250 to 270 metres stands on the house's sheet as the author read it; the house's I Quattro Mori page gives 250 metres on volcanic soil, which agrees.

The house rules: nobody living named (the founder, the professor, the founder's son and a writer met in the sources and not named; a writer's own blog read and never cited); no price, no score (a ranking of 2023 on the house's page was read and not used); British; no dash. The story question asked for the professor's university, which the sources do not settle; it now asks what became of the grapes before 1985, the house's own account, with four fates of one kind.

tested: The founding: the house's history (read through search) gives 1979, two brothers at Montefiascone, to revive the old grapes of the area; Wikipedia and Simpatico Melograno agree; one shop gives 1989. Confirmed.
The 1960s: the house's history has two growers of the family at Monterubiaglio building the family's first cellar in the Sixties. Confirmed; they are described, not named, for want of dates.
The journey of 1988: the house's history says a visit to Bordeaux in 1988 gave one of the two brothers the wish to make a red in Lazio, not both; fixed.

The Merlot clone of 1990: neither the house's history nor its Montiano and Sodale pages and sheets, read through two searches, mention a clone or 1990; the history says small lots of Merlot were tried in vineyard and cellar before the first Montiano of 1993. Cut from the grapes, the story, the card and both explanations.

The first Montiano of 1993: the house's history, DoctorWine's vertical and La Famiglia agree. Confirmed. Its rank: Vinelog lists the 1993 and 1994 vintages as Vino da Tavola, and the Lazio IGT was not yet in being; the house's sheets read Lazio IGT (1999, 2013) and Lazio IGP (2017). The story now says sold outside the DOC rules, later under the regional Lazio IGT.

The sites and the making: the house's sheets give 300 metres on volcanic soil at Montefiascone and Castiglione in Teverina, and BWined agrees on the two places and the volcanic soil; about a year in new barriques by the house and a merchant. Confirmed.

Marciliano: Simpatico Melograno and the house give the purchase of 1999 in the hills south of Orvieto, in the communes of Montecchio and Baschi in Umbria, and DoctorWine and Hellotaste the newer cellar at Montecchio, opened in 2004 by one. Confirmed.
The handover of 2016 to the founders' daughters and the trade name Famiglia Cotarella: the house's sustainability report of 2024 and its history. Confirmed.

Poggio dei Gelsi: Tannico and Xtrawine give it as Est! Est!! Est!!! di Montefiascone Classico DOC; the legend of the bishop and his servant is told as a legend, the bishop not named. Sodale: the house's sheet calls it the second wine of several Merlot vineyards, so it now stands first among the others.

The house rules: nobody living named (the founders, on people.json, and the daughters, not named); no price, no score (the house's line that the 1993 was named among the world's best Merlots in 1995 is not used); British; no dash. The questions: one key each; the explanations teach.

tested: The founding: Vinoway, MangiaeBevi and the house give 1967 at Le Ferriere, the founder from Amatrice; one account places Le Ferriere in the commune of Aprilia, so the place stays near Latina. Confirmed.

Mater Matuta: the house's page (read through search) gives Syrah on native yeasts for 18 to 20 days under a submerged cap with several délestages, the Petit Verdot punched down, 22 to 24 months in oak, first fill barriques, the two apart, then 10 to 12 months in bottle; Ferrowine and Etilika agree on about 85 per cent Syrah, 22 to 24 months in new French oak and 10 to 12 in bottle. Confirmed; others give 6 to 8 or 18 to 24 months in bottle, so about a year stands on the house.

The goddess and the temple: the house's page names the Italic goddess of the dawn, of fertility and of birth and her temple at Satricum close to Le Ferriere; the University of Amsterdam's pages say the dig of 1896 began under a French archaeologist of the École française de Rome and, after two weeks, was taken over by the Italian state's own officials, and another account names an Italian director for 1896 to 1898. The story and the explanation now say digging begun by a French archaeologist uncovered the temple; the card says near Le Ferriere.
The Lapis Satricanus: the University of Amsterdam gives the Dutch return of 1977 and the find in the first week, and Wikipedia agrees. Confirmed.

The reclamation: a paper in Social and Cultural Geography dates the groundwork to 1927 and Britannica the national law to 1928; Littoria was inaugurated in December 1932 and renamed Latina after 1945. Confirmed as the record has it.

The research of 1985: Vinoway and Wine Meridian give a project authorised by the Lazio region's department of agriculture, fifty seven varieties planted, Italian and foreign, and, by the estate's account, Chardonnay, Sauvignon, Syrah, Petit Verdot and Cabernet Sauvignon admitted as recommended varieties from 1990, about twenty kept; MangiaeBevi gives 1988 for the start, against most. The record's close to sixty and early results were loose (the house's own pages differ on which reds came first); now fifty seven and the recommended grapes of 1990, by the house's account.
Anthium: WineNews and Wine Meridian give the Bellone project at Anzio from 2012 and the ungrafted vines. Confirmed.

The house rules: nobody living named (the founder's son, the house's chief, met in an interview's title, not named); no price, no score (the house's awards page with scores read and not used); British; no dash. The questions: one key each; the story question's explanation fixed to the dig's account.

swaps.proposed: The author kept the plan's words, Vigna Adriana, in a wine name reading Donna Adriana, earlier labelled Vigna Adriana, and proposed a swap of the wine's name alone to Donna Adriana, keeping the house and the key, since the house's own pages name the white Donna Adriana.
swaps.why: The house's own story lists Donna Adriana among its three whites of 1993 and its product page sells it as Lazio IGT, Viognier about four fifths with Malvasia del Lazio; Vigna Adriana is the name of listings from 1997 to the early 2000s, some of them labelled Frascati (Lavinium, CellarTracker), one Lazio Bianco IGT (World of Fine Wine). The wine a guest meets and the house leads with is Donna Adriana, so the brief's ground for a swap, a flagship the house does not lead with under that name, is met. Every fact of the record already stands on the house's pages for Donna Adriana or on the facts the refuter checked; the old name stays in the label term, the story and a trap, hedged as the early vintages. The house, the producerId and the key are kept, as in the Capichera and Mas Amiel rulings; no id of wave two is frozen.

swapNote: One swap proposed, by the author, of the wine's name only; accepted with its patch. No other pick is in doubt: Fontana Candida, Falesco, Casale della Ioria and Casale del Giglio are real houses of their appellations, each making the wine the record tells, which their own pages and independent accounts bear out.
planNotes: fontana-candida: the note is answered in part: the blend by the house is Malvasia del Lazio (Puntinata), Malvasia di Candia and Greco, with Trebbiano in older vintages (2004 and 2015 by two listings); no source gives the vineyard's first vintage; Luna Mater is the house's Frascati Superiore DOCG Riserva. The why stands.

castel-de-paolis: the note is answered: the research from 1985 (to 1993 by the house, to 1992 by others), the replanting of 1988 to 1993, the first wines of 1993, Donna Adriana a Lazio IGT. The why is loose: Vigna Adriana is the older name, its early vintages labelled Frascati, and the Viognier led white is Donna Adriana; the swap's planWhy replaces it.

falesco: the note is answered: founded in 1979 at Montefiascone, the first Montiano of 1993, Lazio IGT on the house's sheets and IGP on later ones, with Vino da Tavola for 1993 and 1994 in one listing. The why stands; sold as a Lazio IGT holds for all but the first vintages.

casale-della-ioria: the note is answered: 1921 is not on the house's pages and stays out; the vineyard (Acuto, 335 metres, planted 1986, Guyot) and the ageing (six to eight months in barriques by the house) are the house's sheets. The why's roots it dates to 1921 is loose: the house does not date itself on its pages read, and the importer gives the year; the why's Acuto family estate is loose too, since the cellar stands on the road between Anagni and Paliano and the vines lie at Anagni, Acuto and Piglio.

casale-del-giglio: the note is answered: 1967, Syrah about 85 per cent with Petit Verdot, the temple at Satricum close to Le Ferriere. The why's a sanctuary found on the estate is loose: the house places the temple beside its vineyards, near Le Ferriere, not on the estate.
